query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten (W) particles or regions with a thin, uniform nickel (Ni) film prior to copper (Cu) infiltration will improve interfacial wetting and bonding, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation while preserving mechanical durability under irradiation, relative to conventional processing without an interlayer.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite fabricated by conventional techniques, where W particles or connected W regions are embedded in a Cu matrix, but with significant interfacial defects (voids, poor wetting) that impair thermal transport and mechanical integrity.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin Ni interlayer on the surface of W particles via vapor deposition or sputtering before performing the Cu infiltration or sintering process.
generation.conditions: Processing below temperatures that could trigger interlayer degradation (e.g., <1100–1300 °C) and service under reactor joint conditions typical for fusion devices (high thermal flux and irradiation exposure).
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform Ni interlayer at the W–Cu interface that reduces interfacial energy differences, leading to improved wetting, minimized void formation, and enhanced microstructural continuity.
generation.mechanism: The Ni layer acts as a bonding agent that enhances the infiltration of Cu into the W framework by lowering the energy barrier for wetting. This promotes complete filling of microvoids and reduces phase separation during cooling, resulting in a more uniform and mechanically robust interface that can better transport heat even under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will display a lower void volume fraction, improved thermal conductivity (due to enhanced interfacial contact), and retained mechanical durability under irradiation relative to composites fabricated without the Ni interlayer.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites produced via conventional methods (induction or arc-plasma casting, spark plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, or vapor deposition without interfacial modification) that exhibit interfacial defects and suboptimal thermal/mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Improvement is expected under processing temperatures not exceeding the stability range of the Ni interlayer (typically below 1100–1300 °C) and within service conditions representative of fusion reactor joint environments (high heat flux and ion irradiation conditions as in divertor regions).
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical properties remain to be determined, and potential interdiffusion or reaction between Ni and Cu at elevated temperatures may affect long-term performance; these aspects require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with W particles pre-coated with a thin Ni film and one without (baseline). After Cu infiltration and sintering under controlled conditions, subject both sample sets to identical thermal cycling and irradiation protocols replicating fusion-relevant service conditions. Evaluate interfacial quality, void content, thermal conductivity, and mechanical strength.
measurements: Void volume fraction via X-ray tomography or SEM imaging
Interfacial microstructure characterization with electron microscopy
Thermal conductivity tests (e.g., laser flash analysis)
Mechanical strength tests (e.g., flexural or compression testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not show statistically significant improvements in void reduction, thermal transport, and mechanical durability compared to the baseline after processing and irradiation, the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed.
